items.stem: In February 1919 the newly elected National Assembly met in the town of Weimar. Describe the main features of the Weimar Constitution.
items.answer: The President was elected every seven years and could use Article 48 in an emergency. The Reichstag was elected every four years by proportional representation. All men and women over 20 could vote. The Chancellor needed the support of the Reichstag. A Bill of Rights guaranteed freedoms such as speech and religion.

items.stem: Describe the events of the Munich Putsch in 1923.
items.answer: On 8 November 1923 Hitler and the SA burst into a meeting in a Munich beer hall. He forced Bavarian leaders to agree to support him at gunpoint. The next day Hitler, Ludendorff and about 2,000 Nazis marched through Munich. Police opened fire and sixteen Nazis were killed. Hitler was arrested, tried and given a short prison sentence.

items.stem: In February 1919 the newly elected National Assembly met in the town of Weimar. ‘The Weimar Republic was doomed from the start.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It was linked to defeat and the hated Treaty of Versailles. Proportional representation and Article 48 were weaknesses. It faced violent opposition from left and right. Elites in the army and civil service did not support it. Against: It survived the crises of 1919-23. It recovered under Stresemann in 1924-29. Moderate parties won most votes in the 1920s. It collapsed only after the Depression of 1929. Judgement: The Republic had serious weaknesses from the start, but its survival and recovery in the 1920s show it was not doomed; the Depression was needed to bring it down.

items.stem: Gustav Stresemann was Chancellor in 1923 and Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in 1929. Describe Stresemann's achievements in foreign policy.
items.answer: He agreed the Dawes Plan (1924), which reduced annual reparations and brought US loans. He signed the Locarno Treaties (1925), improving relations with France and Britain. Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926 as a permanent Council member. Germany signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928. He negotiated the Young Plan (1929), reducing the reparations total.

items.stem: The years 1924-29 are often called the “golden years” of the Weimar Republic. (a) Describe the cultural changes in Weimar Germany in the 1920s. [4] (b) Why was the recovery of 1924-29 fragile? [6]
items.answer: (a) Censorship was relaxed and there was more artistic freedom. The Bauhaus pioneered modern architecture and design. German cinema flourished, for example the film Metropolis (1927). Cabaret and nightclubs in Berlin became famous. Some conservatives saw these changes as immoral and un-German. (b) It depended on short-term American loans that could be recalled. Farmers faced falling prices and debt. Unemployment never fell much below a million. Extremist parties still existed and many Germans remained hostile to democracy. Governments were short-lived coalitions.

items.stem: Gustav Stresemann was Chancellor in 1923 and Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in 1929. ‘The Weimar Republic made a full recovery under Stresemann.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Hyperinflation was ended and the currency was stable. Industrial output recovered and living standards rose for many. Germany was accepted back into the international community. Extremist parties lost support: the Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928. Against: The economy relied on American loans. Farmers and some of the middle class did not share in the recovery. Coalition governments remained unstable. Hindenburg, elected President in 1925, was not committed to democracy. Judgement: The recovery was real but fragile, depending on American money and a fragile political consensus, as the Depression showed.

items.stem: On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg appointed Hitler as Chancellor. ‘The Depression was the main reason why Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Unemployment rose to about six million, making voters desperate. Nazi support rose from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.3% in July 1932. Weimar governments were discredited by their failure to deal with it. Against: Nazi propaganda and Hitler's speaking skills won support. Fear of communism pushed industrialists and the middle class to the Nazis. Hitler was appointed through a backstairs deal by Papen and Hindenburg. Weaknesses of the Weimar system, such as Article 48, had already undermined democracy. Judgement: The Depression created the conditions for Nazi success, but Hitler became Chancellor because conservative politicians chose to appoint him.

items.stem: Describe the persecution of Jews in Germany between 1933 and 1939.
items.answer: A boycott of Jewish shops was organised in April 1933. Jews were dismissed from the civil service and professions. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 removed citizenship and banned mixed marriages. During Kristallnacht in 1938 synagogues and shops were destroyed and about 30,000 Jewish men were sent to camps. Jewish children were expelled from schools and Jewish businesses were taken over.

items.stem: (a) Describe how the Nazis tried to control young people. [4] (b) Why did the Nazis persecute minorities? [6]
items.answer: (a) Boys joined the Hitler Youth and girls the League of German Maidens. Membership became compulsory from 1936 and was enforced more strictly from 1939. Activities included camping, sport and military training for boys. The school curriculum was changed to teach Nazi ideas, including race studies. Teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers' League. (b) Nazi racial ideas held that Aryans were a master race and others were inferior. Hitler blamed Jews for Germany's defeat and economic problems. Persecution created a scapegoat that united the “national community” They wanted a racially “pure” and healthy population, so disabled people, Roma and others were targeted.

items.answer: For: Unemployment fell dramatically and many families felt secure. Strength Through Joy provided leisure and holidays. Many took pride in Germany's restored power. items.stem: The years 1924-29 are often called the “golden years” of the Weimar Republic. (a) Describe Stresemann's achievements in foreign policy. [4] (b) ‘The Weimar Republic made a full recovery under Stresemann.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) He agreed the Dawes Plan (1924), which reduced annual reparations and brought US loans. He signed the Locarno Treaties (1925), improving relations with France and Britain. Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926 as a permanent Council member. Germany signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928. He negotiated the Young Plan (1929), reducing the reparations total. (b) For: Hyperinflation was ended and the currency was stable. Industrial output recovered and living standards rose for many. Germany was accepted back into the international community. Extremist parties lost support: the Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928. Against: The economy relied on American loans. Farmers and some of the middle class did not share in the recovery. Coalition governments remained unstable. Hindenburg, elected President in 1925, was not committed to democracy. Judgement: The recovery was real but fragile, depending on American money and a fragile political consensus, as the Depression showed.

items.stem: Describe how Hitler consolidated his power between 1933 and 1934.
items.answer: The Reichstag Fire was used to arrest communists and suspend civil rights. The Enabling Act (March 1933) let Hitler pass laws without the Reichstag. After Hindenburg died, Hitler became Führer and the army swore an oath to him.

items.stem: Opposition to the Nazis existed, but it was small and divided. How effective was opposition to the Nazis? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The July Bomb Plot came close to killing Hitler. Church protests helped stop the official T4 euthanasia programme in 1941. Youth groups showed that not all young people accepted Nazi ideas. Against: Opposition was small, divided and easily crushed. Most Germans conformed or supported the regime. items.stem: How successful were Nazi policies towards young people? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Millions joined the Hitler Youth and many enjoyed its activities. Schools taught Nazi ideas and many young people supported the regime. Against: Some rebelled, for example the Edelweiss Pirates and the Swing Youth. Compulsion suggests voluntary membership was not enough. Some found the activities boring and military drill unpopular. Judgement: Nazi youth policies were largely successful in winning young people's loyalty, but they never achieved total control.
